claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Mutations in CTCF are linked to human disease.
claims.source: Aberrant higher-order chromatin organization can result in abnormal patterns of transcription, and mutations in CTCF are linked to human disease (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).

claims.claim: CTCF binds to a nucleotide motif in HTLV-1 when the virus is integrated as the provirus into the host cell genome.
claims.source: Recently we found (Satou et al., 2016) that CTCF binds to a nucleotide motif in the Human T lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1; also known as the human T-cell leukemia virus), when HTLV-1 is integrated - as the provirus - into the host cell genome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Satou et al., 2016).

claims.claim: HTLV-1 infects ~10 million people in the tropics and subtropics.
claims.source: HTLV-1 is a primate retrovirus that infects ~10 million people in the tropics and subtropics (Bangham, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Bangham, 2018).

claims.claim: The infection is asymptomatic in ~90% of HTLV-1-infected hosts.
claims.source: The infection is asymptomatic in ~90% of human hosts; the remaining 10% of HTLV-1-infected hosts develop either a chronic inflammatory disease, most commonly involving the central nervous system, or an aggressive malignancy of CD4+ T cells known as adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL).
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 infection outcomes.

claims.claim: The remaining 10% of HTLV-1-infected hosts develop either a chronic inflammatory disease or adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL).
claims.source: The infection is asymptomatic in ~90% of human hosts; the remaining 10% of HTLV-1-infected hosts develop either a chronic inflammatory disease, most commonly involving the central nervous system, or an aggressive malignancy of CD4+ T cells known as adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL).
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 disease outcomes.

claims.claim: There is no satisfactory treatment for either the inflammatory or malignant diseases caused by HTLV-1.
claims.source: Unlike HIV-1 infection, there remains no satisfactory treatment for either the inflammatory or malignant diseases caused by HTLV-1.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the current state of HTLV-1 treatment.

claims.claim: A typical host of HTLV-1 carries between 10^4 and 10^5 clones of infected T cells.
claims.source: A typical host of HTLV-1 carries between 104 and 105 clones of infected T cells, each clone carrying a single copy of the provirus in a unique genomic location (Laydon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Laydon et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Each HTLV-1-infected T cell clone carries a single copy of the provirus in a unique genomic location.
claims.source: A typical host of HTLV-1 carries between 104 and 105 clones of infected T cells, each clone carrying a single copy of the provirus in a unique genomic location (Laydon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Laydon et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The large number of HTLV-1-infected clones is established early in infection.
claims.source: The large number of HTLV-1-infected clones appears to be established early in infection, after which persistent clonal proliferation maintains a stable hierarchy of HTLV-1-infected clones for the remainder of the host's life.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 infection dynamics.

claims.claim: Persistent clonal proliferation maintains a stable hierarchy of HTLV-1-infected clones for the remainder of the host's life.
claims.source: The large number of HTLV-1-infected clones appears to be established early in infection, after which persistent clonal proliferation maintains a stable hierarchy of HTLV-1-infected clones for the remainder of the host's life.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 infection dynamics.

claims.claim: Tax and HBZ play indispensable roles in HTLV-1 pathogenesis.
claims.source: The viral regulatory proteins, Tax and HBZ (HTLV-1 bZIP), which are encoded respectively by the sense and antisense strands of the provirus, play indispensable roles in pathogenesis (Matsuoka and Jeang, 2011a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Matsuoka and Jeang, 2011a).

claims.claim: Tax is encoded by the sense strand of the HTLV-1 provirus.
claims.source: The viral regulatory proteins, Tax and HBZ (HTLV-1 bZIP), which are encoded respectively by the sense and antisense strands of the provirus, play indispensable roles in pathogenesis (Matsuoka and Jeang, 2011a).
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 gene organization.

claims.claim: HBZ is encoded by the antisense strand of the HTLV-1 provirus.
claims.source: The viral regulatory proteins, Tax and HBZ (HTLV-1 bZIP), which are encoded respectively by the sense and antisense strands of the provirus, play indispensable roles in pathogenesis (Matsuoka and Jeang, 2011a).
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HTLV-1 gene organization.

claims.claim: Tax is a transcriptional transactivator which dysregulates many host genes.
claims.source: Tax is a transcriptional transactivator which dysregulates many host genes, while HBZ acts as a negative regulator of Tax-mediated host gene transcription and viral expression.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about Tax function.

claims.claim: HBZ acts as a negative regulator of Tax-mediated host gene transcription and viral expression.
claims.source: Tax is a transcriptional transactivator which dysregulates many host genes, while HBZ acts as a negative regulator of Tax-mediated host gene transcription and viral expression.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about HBZ function.

claims.claim: Both Tax and HBZ contribute to persistent proliferation of the infected T cell in vivo.
claims.source: Both Tax and HBZ contribute to persistent proliferation of the infected T cell in vivo, and it is now thought that the consequent accumulation of replicative mutations is a key driver in HTLV-1 oncogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about Tax and HBZ function in HTLV-1 pathogenesis.

claims.claim: The accumulation of replicative mutations is a key driver in HTLV-1 oncogenesis.
claims.source: Both Tax and HBZ contribute to persistent proliferation of the infected T cell in vivo, and it is now thought that the consequent accumulation of replicative mutations is a key driver in HTLV-1 oncogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim represents current scientific thinking about HTLV-1 oncogenesis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Until recently, insertional mutagenesis has not been considered important in causing ATL.
claims.source: However, until recently (Cook et al., 2014; Kataoka et al., 2015; Rosewick et al., 2017) insertional mutagenesis has not been considered important in causing ATL.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work (Cook et al., 2014; Kataoka et al., 2015; Rosewick et al., 2017) that changed this view.

claims.claim: CTCF bound to the HTLV-1 provirus can form abnormal chromatin loops by dimerizing with CTCF in the flanking host genome.
claims.source: The observation that CTCF binds to the HTLV-1 provirus (Satou et al., 2016) raised the hypothesis that CTCF bound to the provirus can form abnormal chromatin loops by dimerizing with CTCF in the flanking host genome.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis raised by the observation that CTCF binds to the provirus.

claims.claim: A single CTCF-dependent chromatin loop was demonstrated in a long-term in vitro T cell line using 3C.
claims.source: Using chromosome conformation capture (3C), we previously demonstrated the presence of a single CTCF-dependent chromatin loop in a long-term in vitro T cell line (Satou et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Satou et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The HTLV-1 provirus forms reproducible abnormal chromatin contacts with sites in the host genome in cis as far as 1.4 Mb from the provirus.
claims.source: We show that the HTLV-1 provirus forms reproducible abnormal chromatin contacts with sites in the host genome in cis as far as 1.4 Mb from the provirus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the q4C data presented in the manuscript, as shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Some abnormal chromatin contacts between the HTLV-1 provirus and host genome depend on CTCF binding to the provirus.
claims.source: Some of these abnormal chromatin contacts depend on CTCF binding to the provirus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: The HTLV-1 provirus causes bidirectional transcription in the host genome immediately flanking the provirus.
claims.source: We show that the provirus causes two distinct patterns of abnormal transcription of the host genome in cis: bidirectional transcription in the host genome immediately flanking the provirus, and clone-specific transcription in cis at non-contiguous loci up to >300 kb from the integration site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The HTLV-1 provirus causes clone-specific transcription in cis at non-contiguous loci up to >300 kb from the integration site.
claims.source: We show that the provirus causes two distinct patterns of abnormal transcription of the host genome in cis: bidirectional transcription in the host genome immediately flanking the provirus, and clone-specific transcription in cis at non-contiguous loci up to >300 kb from the integration site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: HTLV-1 causes insertional mutagenesis up to the megabase range in the host genome in >10^4 persistently-maintained HTLV-1+ T-cell clones in vivo.
claims.source: We conclude that HTLV-1 causes insertional mutagenesis up to the megabase range in the host genome in >104 persistently-maintained HTLV-1+ T-cell clones in vivo.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data showing long-range chromatin contacts and transcriptional changes, combined with knowledge that typical hosts carry 10^4-10^5 infected clones.

claims.claim: Reproducible q4C peaks were detected in 9 of the 10 infected T-cell clones examined.
claims.source: We detected reproducible q4C peaks (long-range chromatin contacts between the provirus and the host genome) in 9 of the 10 infected T-cell clones examined (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1–10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the q4C data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The number of q4C peaks per clone varied between 0 and 15, with a median of 3 peaks per clone.
claims.source: The number of peaks per clone varied between 0 and 15, with a median of 3 peaks per clone (Figure 1C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: There were significantly more q4C peaks downstream of the integration site than upstream.
claims.source: There were significantly more peaks downstream of the integration site than upstream (p=0.03, Chi-squared goodness-of-fit test; Figure 1—figure supplement 11A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the q4C data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 11A.

claims.claim: The distance between identified q4C peaks and the provirus varied between 12.9 kb and 1.4 Mb, with a median of 85 kb.
claims.source: The distance between identified peaks and the provirus of the respective clone varied between 12.9 kb and 1.4 Mb, with a median of 85 kb (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The distance between each q4C peak and the integration site did not significantly differ between upstream and downstream peaks.
claims.source: The distance between each peak and the integration site did not significantly differ between upstream and downstream peaks (p=0.13, Wilcoxon test; Figure 1—figure supplement 11B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 11B.

claims.claim: The HTLV-1 provirus is present in a single copy per cell.
claims.source: The provirus is present in a single copy per cell (Figure 2A) (Cook et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Cook et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The ligation events detected by q4C were confined to a single strand (monoallelic) with a range of at least 4 Mb from the provirus.
claims.source: The alleles identified at heterozygous SNPs in q4C reads demonstrated that the observed ligation events were confined to a single strand (i.e. were monoallelic), with a range of at least 4 Mb from the provirus (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the allelic imbalance analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The infected chromosome could be distinguished from the uninfected chromosome for at least 100 kb either side of the integration site in 8 of the 10 clones.
claims.source: In this way, the infected chromosome could be distinguished from the uninfected chromosome for at least 100 kb either side of the integration site in 8 of the 10 clones (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1–5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the haplotype analysis shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The reproducible contacts between the host genome and the HTLV-1 provirus were exclusively made in cis, on the infected chromosome.
claims.source: The results (Figure 2C) showed that the reproducible contacts between the host genome and the HTLV-1 provirus were exclusively made in cis, that is, on the infected chromosome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the haplotype-specific analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: ~50% of q4C peaks overlapped with at least one CTCF binding site.
claims.source: The results showed that that CTCF-BS were enriched at the chromatin contacts in the host genome: ~50% of q4C peaks overlapped with at least one CTCF-BS (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ChIP-seq and q4C data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In 10% of q4C peaks there were two CTCF binding sites.
claims.source: in 10% of peaks there were two CTCF-BS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ChIP-seq and q4C data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The frequency of CTCF binding sites overlapping the observed q4C peaks was significantly higher than random expectation.
claims.source: The frequency of CTCF-BS overlapping the observed 4C peaks was significantly higher than random expectation (p=4.73 * 10−4, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Where a q4C peak overlapped a CTCF binding site, the viral and host CTCF binding motifs were present in convergent or tandem orientation in 80% of cases.
claims.source: Consistent with recent findings by others (de Wit et al., 2015; Sanborn et al., 2015), where a peak overlapped a CTCF-BS the viral and host CTCF binding motifs were present in convergent or tandem orientation in 80% of cases (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the orientation analysis shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with cited literature (de Wit et al., 2015; Sanborn et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The presence of a CTCF binding site was associated with a significantly greater observed q4C peak height.
claims.source: The presence of a CTCF-BS was associated with a significantly greater observed q4C peak height (p=0.025, Wilcoxon test)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the q4C data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There was a significant positive trend between the q4C peak height and the number of CTCF sites within the peak.
claims.source: there was a significant positive trend between the q4C peak height and the number of CTCF sites within the peak (Figure 3C; p=0.016, Spearman's test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the number of observed chromatin contacts in a clone and the number of CTCF binding sites within 0.5 Mb of the integration site.
claims.source: Finally, there was a significant positive correlation between the number of observed chromatin contacts in a clone and the number of CTCF-BS within 0.5 Mb of the integration site (Figure 3D; Pearson's correlation test)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: This correlation between chromatin contacts and CTCF binding sites remained significant up to 1.16 Mb from the provirus.
claims.source: this correlation remained significant up to 1.16 Mb from the provirus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the q4C and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The loss of CTCF binding was associated with a loss of 5 of the eight observed contacts in CRISPR-modified clones.
claims.source: The results show that the loss of CTCF binding was associated with a loss of 5 of the eight observed contacts; three of the five lost contacts overlapped a CTCF-BS in the host.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: Three of the five lost contacts after CTCF knockout overlapped a CTCF binding site in the host.
claims.source: The results show that the loss of CTCF binding was associated with a loss of 5 of the eight observed contacts; three of the five lost contacts overlapped a CTCF-BS in the host.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: Upregulated transcription was observed in the host genome immediately flanking the HTLV-1 provirus in all clones examined.
claims.source: The results showed upregulated transcription in the host genome immediately flanking the HTLV-1 provirus, in all clones examined (Figure 4A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1–10, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Upregulated transcription was observed either upstream or downstream of the provirus, or both, with a predominant increase downstream in the same sense as the HTLV-1 plus-strand and upstream in the opposite sense.
claims.source: This upregulated transcription was observed either upstream or downstream of the provirus, or both, with a predominant increase downstream in the same sense as the HTLV-1 plus-strand and upstream in the opposite sense (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Abnormal upstream antisense expression was present in most clones.
claims.source: The results showed that, whereas abnormal upstream antisense expression was present in most clones, an increase in same-sense transcription was specific to those clones with high plus-strand expression (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: An increase in same-sense transcription was specific to those clones with high plus-strand expression.
claims.source: The results showed that, whereas abnormal upstream antisense expression was present in most clones, an increase in same-sense transcription was specific to those clones with high plus-strand expression (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In clone TBX4B, HTLV-1 is inserted between exons of the gene PNPLA.
claims.source: For example, in clone TBX4B, HTLV-1 is inserted between exons of the gene PNPLA (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the integration site data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The gene PNPLA was not expressed in the other T cell clones, but was highly expressed in TBX4B both downstream and upstream of the integration site, in the same sense as the proviral plus-strand.
claims.source: This gene was not expressed in the other T cell clones, but was highly expressed in TBX4B both downstream and upstream of the integration site, in the same sense as the proviral plus-strand.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data for clone TBX4B shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The presence of abnormal same-sense host transcription upstream of the 5′ LTR suggests that the transcription was driven by the proviral enhancer.
claims.source: The presence of abnormal same-sense host transcription upstream of the 5′ LTR suggests that the transcription was driven by the proviral enhancer.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of upstream same-sense transcription.

claims.claim: In clone 8.8, there was upregulation of host transcription both flanking the integration site and in the gene TBC1D4 ~44 kb upstream.
claims.source: For example, in clone 8.8, there was upregulation of host transcription both flanking the integration site and in the gene TBC1D4 (a Rab GTPase-activating protein) ~44 kb upstream; no transcripts were detected in the intervening host genome (Figure 4B, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: No transcripts were detected in the intervening host genome between the integration site and TBC1D4 in clone 8.8.
claims.source: For example, in clone 8.8, there was upregulation of host transcription both flanking the integration site and in the gene TBC1D4 (a Rab GTPase-activating protein) ~44 kb upstream; no transcripts were detected in the intervening host genome (Figure 4B, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Non-contiguous transcription occurred at the downstream contact site made with the provirus in clone 8.8, resulting in aberrant splicing of the gene UCHL3 to produce putative novel UCHL3 transcripts.
claims.source: Non-contiguous transcription also occurred at the downstream contact site made with the provirus, resulting in aberrant splicing of the gene UCHL3 to produce putative novel UCHL3 transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In clone 3.60, abnormal non-contiguous transcription was found downstream of the provirus between the provirus and the contact formed with the host genome.
claims.source: In clone 3.60, abnormal non-contiguous transcription was found downstream of the provirus (Figure 4B, right) between the provirus and the contact (indicated by the q4C peak) formed with the host genome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq and q4C data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The abnormal transcription observed in clone 3.60 was present in the positive strand with alternative splicing, resulting in a putative novel transcript of SULT1B1.
claims.source: This region contains a gene (SULT1B1) in the negative strand of the genome; the abnormal transcription observed in clone 3.60 was present in the positive strand with alternative splicing, resulting in a putative novel transcript (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The provirus can alter transcription in cis both within and between genes, and alter splicing, producing novel transcripts.
claims.source: These observations demonstrate that the provirus can alter transcription in cis both within and between genes, and alter splicing, producing novel transcripts.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing altered transcription and splicing patterns.

claims.claim: In heterozygous SNPs identified in the clone-specific transcripts, transcription was predominantly homozygous (monoallelic).
claims.source: The results showed that in heterozygous SNPs identified in the clone-specific transcripts, transcription was predominantly homozygous, that is, monoallelic (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the allelic imbalance analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Where the transcripts could be assigned to one chromosome, the observed clone-specific transcripts were overwhelmingly derived from the infected chromosome.
claims.source: The results (Figure 5B,C,D) showed that, where the transcripts could be assigned to one chromosome, the observed clone-specific transcripts were overwhelmingly derived from the infected chromosome, whereas transcripts that were not specifically upregulated were expressed from either chromosome at a similar frequency (Figure 5B, left side of left panel; Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the haplotype-specific RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claims.claim: Transcripts that were not specifically upregulated were expressed from either chromosome at a similar frequency.
claims.source: The results (Figure 5B,C,D) showed that, where the transcripts could be assigned to one chromosome, the observed clone-specific transcripts were overwhelmingly derived from the infected chromosome, whereas transcripts that were not specifically upregulated were expressed from either chromosome at a similar frequency (Figure 5B, left side of left panel; Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the haplotype-specific RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claims.claim: The mammalian genome is folded in a highly ordered manner at a series of successively larger spatial scales.
claims.source: The mammalian genome is not randomly arranged in the nucleus, but is folded in a highly ordered manner at a series of successively larger spatial scales (Bickmore, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Bickmore, 2013) and represents established knowledge about genome organization.

claims.claim: Chromatin is organized in a series of reproducible loops that are formed by bringing together specific genomic loci which are separated on the linear genome by up to ~2 Mb.
claims.source: At the smallest scale, chromatin is organized in a series of reproducible loops that are formed by bringing together specific genomic loci which are separated on the linear genome by up to ~2 Mb (Dekker and Heard, 2015; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Dekker and Heard, 2015; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012) and represents established knowledge about chromatin organization.

claims.claim: The non-palindromic CTCF binding site is found at the borders of ~80% of chromatin loops.
claims.source: The zinc finger protein CTCF plays a central part in establishing and maintaining these chromatin loops: the non-palindromic CTCF-BS is found at the borders of ~80% of loops.
claims.evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about CTCF's role in chromatin loop formation.

claims.claim: Certain other chromatin-associated proteins, such as PRC1, and transcription factors including AP-1 and YY1, can also cause looping of chromatin.
claims.source: Certain other chromatin-associated proteins, such as PRC1 (Schoenfelder et al., 2015), and transcription factors including AP-1 (Phanstiel et al., 2017) and YY1 (Beagan et al., 2017), can also cause looping of chromatin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Schoenfelder et al., 2015; Phanstiel et al., 2017; Beagan et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Chromatin loops play a critical part in controlling gene expression by regulating the contacts made between enhancers and promoters.
claims.source: The resulting chromatin loops in turn play a critical part in controlling gene expression, by regulating the contacts made between enhancers and promoters (Bartman et al., 2016; Gibcus and Dekker, 2013; Schwarzer and Spitz, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bartman et al., 2016; Gibcus and Dekker, 2013; Schwarzer and Spitz, 2014) and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Disruption of chromatin loops can deregulate gene expression and cause developmental abnormalities.
claims.source: Disruption of chromatin loops can deregulate gene expression and cause developmental abnormalities (Lupiáñez et al., 2015) or diseases such as cancer (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Disruption of chromatin loops can cause diseases such as cancer.
claims.source: Disruption of chromatin loops can deregulate gene expression and cause developmental abnormalities (Lupiáñez et al., 2015) or diseases such as cancer (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Corces and Corces, 2016; Flavahan et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Each clone studied has a unique pattern of chromatin contacts, depending on the site of integration of the provirus in the host genome.
claims.source: Each clone has a unique pattern of chromatin contacts, depending on the site of integration of the provirus in the host genome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the q4C data showing different contact patterns in different clones (Figure 1B and supplementary figures).

claims.claim: The provirus makes preferential contacts in cis with host chromatin at distances at least 4 Mb from the provirus.
claims.source: The allelic bias observed in the q4C data, with the preferential detection of SNPs on the chromosome carrying the provirus, indicates that the provirus makes preferential contacts in cis with host chromatin at distances at least 4 Mb from the provirus.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the allelic bias observed in q4C data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Preferential contacts in cis may extend beyond 4 Mb from the provirus, but detection is likely to be limited by the sensitivity of the q4C technique.
claims.source: Preferential contacts in cis may extend beyond this distance, but detection is likely to be limited by the sensitivity of the q4C technique.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of the technique.

claims.claim: Not all host chromatin contact sites contain CTCF binding sites.
claims.source: However, not all host chromatin contact sites contain CTCF-BS, and certain peaks remained detectable by q4C after knock-out of the proviral CTCF-BS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing that ~50% of peaks contain CTCF-BS (Figure 3A) and that some peaks remain after CTCF knockout (Figure 3E, 3F).

claims.claim: Certain q4C peaks remained detectable after knock-out of the proviral CTCF binding site.
claims.source: However, not all host chromatin contact sites contain CTCF-BS, and certain peaks remained detectable by q4C after knock-out of the proviral CTCF-BS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: These observations are consistent with the findings that certain chromatin-associated proteins other than CTCF can also give rise to chromatin looping.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with the findings that certain chromatin-associated proteins other than CTCF can also give rise to chromatin looping (Schoenfelder et al., 2015; Phanstiel et al., 2017; Beagan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data and is supported by citations (Schoenfelder et al., 2015; Phanstiel et al., 2017; Beagan et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The abnormal chromatin loops might alter the normal contacts made between enhancers and promoters in the host genome, either creating new contacts or abrogating pre-existing contacts.
claims.source: At least two mechanisms of such deregulation can be suggested. First, the abnormal chromatin loops might alter the normal contacts made between enhancers and promoters in the host genome, either creating new contacts or abrogating pre-existing contacts.
claims.evidence: This is a suggested mechanism based on inference from the data.

claims.claim: The new chromatin loop might bring the proviral LTR near a host promoter and cause abnormal transcription from the promoter.
claims.source: Second, the new chromatin loop might bring the proviral LTR near a host promoter and cause abnormal transcription from the promoter.
claims.evidence: This is a suggested mechanism based on inference from the data.

claims.claim: Each clone has a unique pattern of transcription.
claims.source: Again, each clone has a unique pattern of transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Kataoka et al. and Rosewick et al. have reported evidence of transcription initiated on the minus strand of the provirus and continuing upstream into the host genome in transformed lymphocyte clones carrying HTLV-1 or BLV.
claims.source: Kataoka et al. (Kataoka et al., 2015) and Rosewick et al. (Rosewick et al., 2017) have reported evidence of transcription initiated on the minus strand of the provirus and continuing upstream into the host genome in transformed lymphocyte clones carrying HTLV-1 or the related bovine leukemia virus (BLV).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work (Kataoka et al., 2015; Rosewick et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Since the virus infects between 10^4 and 10^5 different clones of T cells in a typical host, each carrying the provirus at a different genomic location, the virus deregulates tens of thousands of host genes in a typical infected host.

results.result: The HTLV-1 provirus forms reproducible chromatin contacts with the host genome detected by q4C in 9 of 10 clones examined, with a median of 3 peaks per clone, ranging from 12.9 kb to 1.4 Mb from the provirus, with significantly more peaks downstream than upstream.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are well-supported by the q4C data presented in Figure 1B-D and supplementary figures. The statistical analyses (chi-squared test for directional bias, Wilcoxon test for distance comparison) are appropriate and support the quantitative claims about peak distribution and distance.

results.result: The chromatin contacts between the HTLV-1 provirus and host genome are monoallelic and occur exclusively in cis on the infected chromosome, as demonstrated by allelic imbalance analysis of heterozygous SNPs in q4C reads extending at least 4 Mb from the provirus.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by the allelic imbalance analysis shown in Figure 2B-C and supplementary figures. The haplotype-specific analysis using heterozygous SNPs provides strong evidence for cis-specific contacts, though the 4 Mb range represents the limit of detection rather than a biological boundary.

results.result: CTCF binding sites are significantly enriched at provirus-host chromatin contact sites, with ~50% of q4C peaks overlapping at least one CTCF-BS, preferentially in convergent or tandem orientation (80%), and the presence and number of CTCF-BS correlate with peak height and frequency of contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 are well-supported by the integrated ChIP-seq and q4C analysis shown in Figure 3A-D. The statistical tests (Fisher's exact test, Wilcoxon test, Spearman's test, Pearson's correlation) are appropriate and demonstrate significant enrichment of CTCF-BS at contact sites. The orientation analysis is consistent with published literature on CTCF-mediated looping.

results.result: CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of the proviral CTCF binding site resulted in loss of 5 of 8 observed chromatin contacts, with 3 of the 5 lost contacts overlapping a CTCF-BS in the host genome, demonstrating that some chromatin contacts depend on CTCF binding to the provirus.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 and C26 are supported by the CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3E-F. The functional validation in two different clones (ED and TBX4B) strengthens the conclusion. However, the fact that not all contacts were lost and some contacts lack CTCF-BS suggests additional mechanisms are involved, which the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: The HTLV-1 provirus causes bidirectional transcriptional upregulation in the immediately flanking host genome in all clones examined, with predominant antisense transcription upstream and same-sense transcription downstream, where same-sense transcription is specific to clones with high plus-strand expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 and C27 are supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A-D and supplementary figures. The bidirectional pattern is consistent across clones, and the correlation with Tax expression (Figure 4D) provides mechanistic insight. The analysis appropriately distinguishes between high and low Tax-expressing clones.

results.result: The HTLV-1 provirus causes clone-specific transcription at non-contiguous loci up to >300 kb from the integration site, including aberrant splicing producing putative novel transcripts, demonstrating that the provirus can alter transcription both within and between genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61, C28, and C85 are supported by the RNA-seq data showing non-contiguous transcription in specific clones (e.g., clone 8.8 with TBC1D4, clone 3.60 with SULT1B1) as shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures. The splice junction analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) provides evidence for aberrant splicing. Each clone shows a unique pattern, supporting the clone-specific nature of these effects.

results.result: Clone-specific transcripts are predominantly monoallelic and derived from the infected chromosome, as demonstrated by allelic imbalance analysis of heterozygous SNPs in RNA-seq reads, while non-upregulated transcripts show biallelic expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 and C86 are supported by the haplotype-specific RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A-D. The allelic imbalance analysis demonstrates that clone-specific upregulated transcripts are monoallelic (AI approaching 0.5) and derived from the infected chromosome, while shared transcripts are biallelic. The statistical analysis (Wilcoxon test, p=6.7×10⁻¹²) is appropriate and highly significant.

results.result: HTLV-1 causes insertional mutagenesis up to the megabase range in the host genome, with chromatin contacts extending to 1.4 Mb and affecting >10⁴ persistently-maintained T-cell clones in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C29, and C100 are supported by the q4C data showing contacts up to 1.4 Mb (Figure 1D) combined with established knowledge that typical hosts carry 10⁴-10⁵ infected clones (C11). The conclusion about megabase-range insertional mutagenesis is a reasonable inference from the data, though the functional consequences require further investigation as the authors acknowledge (C103).

results.result: Chromatin looping between the provirus and host genome is an important mechanism underlying the observed abnormal transcription at distant loci, distinguishing HTLV-1 from other retroviruses like MLV that exploit pre-existing chromatin loops.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C87, and C99 represent inferences based on the combined q4C and RNA-seq data showing both chromatin contacts and transcriptional changes at the same loci. The correlation between contacts and transcriptional changes, along with the monoallelic nature of both phenomena on the infected chromosome, provides strong support for this mechanistic interpretation. The comparison with MLV (C96-C98) appropriately contextualizes the novelty of the findings.

results.result: In clone TBX4B, HTLV-1 integration between exons of PNPLA resulted in clone-specific high expression of this gene both upstream and downstream of the integration site in the same sense as the proviral plus-strand, suggesting transcription driven by the proviral enhancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by the integration site data and RNA-seq analysis for clone TBX4B shown in Figure 3F. The observation of same-sense transcription upstream of the 5' LTR provides evidence for enhancer-driven transcription, though this remains an inference rather than direct demonstration of enhancer activity.

results.result: Each infected T-cell clone has a unique pattern of chromatin contacts and transcription that depends on the proviral integration site and the presence of nearby CTCF binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C80, and C101 are supported by the clone-specific patterns observed in both q4C and RNA-seq data across all 10 clones examined (Figure 1B-C, Figure 4A, supplementary figures). The correlation between CTCF-BS density and contact frequency (C45) supports the role of CTCF-BS location in determining clone-specific patterns.

results.result: Since HTLV-1 infects 10⁴-10⁵ different T-cell clones in a typical host, each with the provirus at a different genomic location, the virus deregulates tens of thousands of host genes in a typical infected host.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 is a reasonable inference based on the demonstrated clone-specific transcriptional changes (multiple genes per clone) combined with established knowledge about the number of infected clones per host (C11). However, this represents an extrapolation from in vitro clones to the in vivo situation, and the actual number of deregulated genes per host would depend on factors not directly measured in this study.

results.result: Not all host chromatin contact sites contain CTCF binding sites, and certain q4C peaks remained detectable after CTCF knockout, consistent with findings that other chromatin-associated proteins can also mediate chromatin looping.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by the data showing that ~50% of peaks lack CTCF-BS (C39) and that some peaks persist after CTCF knockout (Figure 3E-F). The interpretation that other proteins may be involved is appropriately cautious and supported by citations to relevant literature (Schoenfelder et al., 2015; Phanstiel et al., 2017; Beagan et al., 2017).

results.result: Background information on CTCF function, chromatin organization, HTLV-1 biology, and the historical context of insertional mutagenesis in HTLV-1 pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C22 represent established knowledge about CTCF, chromatin organization, and HTLV-1 biology, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide essential context for the study but do not represent new findings from this work.

results.result: Previous work by the authors demonstrated that CTCF binds to the HTLV-1 provirus and showed a single CTCF-dependent chromatin loop in a long-term in vitro T cell line using 3C, raising the hypothesis that CTCF bound to the provirus can form abnormal chromatin loops.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 accurately describe prior work by the authors (Satou et al., 2016) that motivated the current study. The hypothesis is appropriately framed as arising from these prior observations.

results.result: Discussion of established knowledge about genome organization, chromatin looping, retroviral insertional mutagenesis, and comparison with other retroviruses including MLV and foamy virus.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71, C81-C82, C88-C89, C91-C97, C106-C112 represent established knowledge and appropriate contextualization of the findings within the broader literature. These claims are well-supported by citations and provide important context for interpreting the significance of the results.

results.result: The HTLV-1 provirus is present in a single copy per cell in the clones studied.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by citation to prior work (Cook et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 2A. This is an important control establishing that the observed effects are due to a single proviral integration site per clone.

results.result: The provirus makes preferential contacts in cis with host chromatin at distances of at least 4 Mb from the provirus, though contacts may extend beyond this distance limited by the sensitivity of the q4C technique.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is an inference based on the allelic bias in q4C data (Figure 2B), while C74 appropriately acknowledges technical limitations. The 4 Mb range represents the limit of detection rather than a biological boundary, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: Proposed mechanisms for transcriptional deregulation and speculation about CTCF function, with acknowledgment that further work is needed to test these hypotheses and investigate functional consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79, C102-C105, and C90 represent speculative mechanisms and hypotheses for future investigation. While these are reasonable inferences based on the data and established knowledge, they are explicitly presented as speculation or postulates requiring further testing. The authors appropriately acknowledge these as areas for future work.

results.result: Speculation that chance integration of MLV at particular loci enabled the virus to exploit normal chromatin loops present in the mouse genome.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is a speculative inference about MLV mechanisms based on work by Sokol et al. (2014). While plausible, this represents speculation about another virus system rather than a finding from the current study.

results.result: HTLV-1 has the potential to disrupt host gene expression in cis at both contiguous and non-contiguous sites, in addition to the generic effects of Tax on host gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by the RNA-seq data showing both contiguous and non-contiguous transcriptional changes. The distinction from Tax-mediated effects (C111-C112) is appropriate, as the observed effects are clone-specific rather than generic across all infected cells.
